entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4557"/><div sID="gen6598" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4557"/>5. Neither wild animals, as the wild ass, nor tame, as the ox, are dissatisfied when well-supplied with food. The braying of the one and the lowing of the other prove distress and want of palatable food. So, Job argues, if he complains, it is not without cause; namely, his pains, which are, as it were, disgusting food, which God feeds him with (end of <reference osisRef="Job.6.7">Job 6:7</reference>). But he should have remembered a rational being should evince a better spirit than the brute. <div eID="gen6598" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4559"/><div sID="gen6601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4559"/>7. To "touch" is contrasted with "meat." "My taste refused even to touch it, and yet am I fed with such meat of sickness." The second clause literally, is, "Such is like the sickness of my food." The natural taste abhors even to touch insipid food, and such forms my nourishment. For my sickness is like such nauseous food [Umbreit]. (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.3">Psa 42:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.5">80:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.9">102:9</reference>). No wonder, then, I complain. <div eID="gen6601" type="x-p"/>

The second clause literally, is, "Such is like the sickness of my food." The natural taste abhors even to touch insipid food, and such forms my nourishment. For my sickness is like such nauseous food [Umbreit]. ( Psa 42:3 ; 80:5 ; 102:9 ). No wonder, then, I complain.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4566"/><div sID="gen6611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4566"/><hi type="bold">14. pity--</hi>a proverb. Charity is the love which judges indulgently of our fellow men: it is put on a par with truth in <reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">Pr 3:3</reference>, for they together form the essence of moral perfection [Umbreit]. It is the spirit of Christianity (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">1Pe 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.7">1Co 13:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pr 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">17:17</reference>). If it ought to be used towards all men, much more towards friends. But he who does not use it forsaketh (renounceth) the fear of the Almighty (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.13">Jas 2:13</reference>). <div eID="gen6611" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4567"/><div sID="gen6612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4567"/><hi type="bold">15. Those whom I regarded as "my brethren," from whom I looked for faithfulness in my adversity, have disappointed me, as the streams failing from drought--</hi>wadies of Arabia, filled in the winter, but dry in the summer, which disappoint the caravans expecting to find water there. The fulness and noise of these temporary streams answer to the past large and loud professions of my friends; their dryness in summer, to the failure of the friendship when needed. The Arab proverb says of a treacherous friend, "I trust not in thy torrent" (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Is 58:11</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen6612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stream of brooks--</hi>rather, "the brook in the ravines which passes away." It has no perpetual spring of water to renew it (unlike "the fountain of living waters," <reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jr 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">Is 33:16</reference>, at the end); and thus it passes away as rapidly as it arose. <div eID="gen6613" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4570"/><div sID="gen6616" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4570"/><hi type="bold">18. turned aside--</hi>rather, "caravans" (Hebrew, "travellers") turn aside from their way, by circuitous routes, to obtain water. They had seen the brook in spring full of water: and now in the summer heat, on their weary journey, they turn off their road by a devious route to reach the living waters, which they remembered with such pleasure. But, when "they go," it is "into a desert" [Noyes and Umbreit]. Not as English Version, "They go to nothing," which would be a tame repetition of the drying up of the waters in <reference osisRef="Job.6.17">Job 6:17</reference>; instead of waters, they find an "empty wilderness"; and, not having strength to regain their road, bitterly disappointed, they "perish." The terse brevity is most expressive. <div eID="gen6616" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4576"/><div sID="gen6628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4576"/>24-25. Irony. If you can "teach me" the right view, I am willing to be set right, and "hold my tongue"; and to be made to see my error. But then if your words be really the right words, how is it that they are so feeble? "Yet how feeble are the words of what you call the right view." So the Hebrew is used (in <reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">Mi 2:10</reference>; 1:9). The English Version, "How powerful," &c., does not agree so well with the last clause of the verse. <div eID="gen6628" type="x-p"/>
